sections.title: The indefinite and partitive articles with nouns

attestations.section_title: The indefinite and partitive articles with nouns
attestations.source_text: The indefinite articles are un (masculine singular) (a), une (feminine singular) (a), and des (both masculine and feminine plural) (some).
The partitive article is used when the exact quantity of an item is unknown... It is formed by combining de and the definite article. de + le = du; de + l’ = de l’; de + la = de la; de + les = des.

The noun endings very often indicate their gender... Nouns ending in -age, -eau, and -ment tend to be masculine... Nouns ending in -ure, -ence, -ance, -sion, -tion, -té, -ouille, -eille, -ie, -ette, -eur tend to be feminine.
In most cases, an -s is added to a noun to make it plural... Nouns ending in -s, -x, or -z do not change... Nouns ending in -eu, -eau usually take an -x... Nouns ending in -al usually change to -aux.
Countries, continents, states, provinces, and regions also have a gender. For geographical nouns, an -e ending usually indicates the feminine. Other endings tend to be masculine.

To express in or to with a geographical name, the preposition varies. With cities, the preposition à is used... With countries, regions, states, and provinces, the article and/or the preposition change according to gender and number.
From is expressed by de (d’) for continents, feminine countries, provinces, regions, and states. For masculine and plural entities, the definite article is retained (du, des).

grammar_rules.rule_name: Definite article: le, la, l', les
grammar_rules.summary: Use le for masculine singular, la for feminine singular, l' before vowel or mute h, les for plural.
grammar_rules.explanation: French nouns have gender. Definite article agrees in gender and number.
grammar_rules.formation: le + masculine singular; la + feminine singular; l' + vowel/mute h singular; les + plural
usage: to refer to specific nouns
to express general concepts
conditions: before singular nouns starting with vowel or mute h, use l'
agreement_rules: agrees with noun gender and number
common_traps: Do not forget to elide before vowel sound.

attestations.source_text: French uses le for masculine nouns and la for feminine nouns. Le and la are shortened to l’ before a singular noun or adjective that begins with a vowel sound. The plural les is used for both masculine and feminine.

grammar_rules.summary: Use un for masculine singular, une for feminine singular, des for plural.

usage: to refer to non-specific nouns
to indicate one item or some items
agreement_rules: agrees with noun gender and number
grammar_rules.negative_form: In negative, un/une/des often become de (except with être).

grammar_rules.rule_name: Partitive article: du, de la, de l', des
grammar_rules.summary: Use partitive article to express unspecified quantity: du, de la, de l', des.
grammar_rules.explanation: Partitive article is required in French where English often omits 'some'.
grammar_rules.formation: de + le = du; de + l' = de l'; de + la = de la; de + les = des
usage: to indicate an unspecified amount of a mass noun
to indicate some of a plural noun
conditions: used with non-count nouns and plural count nouns when quantity is unknown
exceptions: In negative sentences, du/de la/de l'/des become de (except after être).
agreement_rules: agrees with noun gender and number
grammar_rules.negative_form: du/de la/de l'/des → de (or d' before vowel/mute h)
common_traps: Do not use de after être in negative; keep partitive: Ce n'est pas du fromage.

attestations.source_text: The partitive article is used when the exact quantity of an item is unknown... It is formed by combining de and the definite article. de + le = du; de + l’ = de l’; de + la = de la; de + les = des.

grammar_rules.summary: In negative, du/de la/de l'/des become de (or d').
grammar_rules.explanation: Because quantity doesn't exist, partitive article is replaced by de.
grammar_rules.formation: du/de la/de l'/des → de (or d' before vowel/mute h)
usage: to express negation of existence of mass/plural items
exceptions: C'est du fromage → Ce n'est pas du fromage (être retains partitive)
common_traps: Do not use de after être in negative.

attestations.source_text: When used in the negative, the du, de la, and des all become de, since the quantity of the item doesn’t exist any longer.

usage: to predict gender of nouns

grammar_rules.summary: Use à to express in/to for cities.
grammar_rules.explanation: Cities generally do not take an article and use à.
usage: to express location or direction to a city
restrictions: Some cities have article: Le Caire, La Havane, etc.
common_traps: Do not use en/au for cities.

attestations.source_text: With cities, the preposition à is used. Cities are usually not preceded by an article.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Preposition with countries: en, au, aux
grammar_rules.summary: Use en for feminine countries and masculine starting with vowel; au for masculine; aux for plural.
grammar_rules.explanation: Preposition depends on gender and number of country.
grammar_rules.formation: en + feminine or vowel-starting masculine; au + masculine singular; aux + plural
usage: to express in/to a country
common_traps: Do not use à for countries.

attestations.source_text: en before feminine countries and regions; en before masculine countries beginning with a vowel; au before singular masculine countries; aux before plural countries.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Preposition with states/provinces: en, au, dans le
grammar_rules.summary: Use en for feminine or vowel-starting masculine states; au for masculine; dans le sometimes replaces au.
grammar_rules.explanation: Similar to countries but with variation.
grammar_rules.formation: en + feminine/vowel masculine; au + masculine; dans le + masculine consonant
usage: to express in/to a state or province
common_traps: dans le often replaces au for masculine states starting with consonant.

attestations.source_text: However, with provinces, departments, or states, the preposition may vary. Before feminine nouns or masculine nouns starting with a vowel, use en. Au is used in front of masculine states. In front of masculine nouns starting with a consonant, dans le often replaces au.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Preposition with islands: à, aux, en
grammar_rules.summary: Usually à for islands, aux for plural; exceptions with en.
grammar_rules.explanation: Island usage varies; à is common.
grammar_rules.formation: à + island; aux + plural; en for some exceptions
usage: to express in/to an island
common_traps: Some islands use en, not à.

attestations.source_text: Although usage may vary, the preposition à (aux in the plural) is often used for islands. Some exceptions: en Haïti, en Martinique, en Guadeloupe.

grammar_rules.summary: Use de/d' for continents, feminine countries, provinces, regions, states; du/des for masculine/plural.
grammar_rules.explanation: From is de for feminine and vowel-starting, du/des for masculine/plural.
grammar_rules.formation: de (d') + feminine or vowel masculine; du + masculine singular; des + plural
usage: to express origin or return from a place
common_traps: Use du/des for masculine/plural, not de.
